label: GPT-6 Astra
output:
Peter, your point about HR becoming the lender of first resort is fair. Nine years in payroll will have shown you the recovery problems and the work that an informal scheme creates. I also agree that someone taking an advance every month deserves attention. We should not pretend that paying part of a salary early solves a household income problem.

But I disagree quite strongly with the advice to close the window and assume people will adjust after one or two pay cycles. We tried almost exactly that in 2025, and we had to reverse it.

I work in logistics, with about 340 staff across depots in Embakasi and Changamwe. Most are drivers, turn-boys, loaders and warehouse clerks. We stopped salary advances in February 2025 after Finance raised much the same objections you have: cash flow, dependence, administration and recovery when someone leaves. We gave two months’ notice rather than your suggested three, and held a financial literacy session with the SACCO.

So we did not just withdraw the facility overnight and leave people without an explanation or an alternative.

In the six months afterwards, reception logged **61 calls from debt collectors and loan apps**, up from a handful before. That is 61 calls, not 61 employees, but it was still a very visible change. Some apps were also calling supervisors whom employees had listed as “referees”.

This is where I struggle with the argument that the loan is the employee’s own contract and therefore outside the company’s business. Legally, it is their contract. Operationally, the consequences were reaching reception, supervisors, payroll and HR. Removing our advance facility did not remove the staff time being spent on debt problems. Some of that work simply moved out of the advance approval process, where Finance could see it, into other departments, where it was harder to count.

We also saw an increase in unplanned absence on the two days after month-end. Our fleet manager linked at least three missed Mombasa runs to drivers “sorting out” loans.

I would not claim that every absence was caused by stopping advances, or that those observations amount to a controlled study. They do not. But they were enough to challenge our original assumption that withdrawing the scheme would save time and money without creating costs elsewhere.

One loader at Changamwe had six loan apps running at once by the time he came to me. He was borrowing from one to pay another. It took us four months working with payroll to unwind that situation. That is one person’s case, not a description of everyone who borrows, but it certainly was not a problem that settled itself after two pay cycles.

On the SACCO point, I agree that it has an important role. We still encourage staff to use it. But our SACCO loans take two to three weeks to process and need guarantors. That does not help much when a child is sent home over school fees on a Tuesday.

Financial literacy is useful too. It can help someone plan, understand borrowing costs and avoid a bad loan. It cannot make every emergency affordable on KES 28,000 a month. We need both sensible financial education and an honest view of what the salary can cover.

We reopened advances in September 2025, but we did **not** reopen the old informal arrangement. That distinction is important for Brenda. The choice is not only between “anyone can come to HR and ask” and “no advances under any circumstances”.

Our replacement was a written policy:

- **Maximum advance of 40% of net pay.** That is a ceiling, not an automatic entitlement.
- **Once per pay cycle.** No repeated top-ups during the month.
- **Full repayment at the next payroll.**
- **No fee.**
- **Requests through the payroll portal**, rather than a queue at my office.
- **A check of existing deductions before approval.** The Employment Act limits total deductions to two-thirds of wages, so we check that separately. The 40% net-pay cap does not replace that check, and we do not approve an amount that leaves someone with nothing at month-end.

Since reopening, we have been handling about 55–70 requests a month, averaging around KES 9,000. That gives Finance a sense of the normal volume: roughly KES 495,000–630,000 passing through the scheme in a month at that average. That is money paid early and recovered through payroll, not a monthly expense of that amount. It still needs to be planned for.

On recovery, we recovered everything except balances from two leavers, with roughly KES 14,000 written off for the year.

So your warning about leavers is valid. We have an actual loss against that risk, and I would not tell Brenda to promise her Finance Manager that recovery will always be 100%. But I would ask Finance to compare that loss, plus the administration involved, with the other costs we experienced: absence, missed runs, reception calls and supervisors’ time. Those costs matter even when they do not appear against the salary advance scheme.

Our Finance Manager now defends the scheme himself. What changed his position was having written limits and a forecastable exposure. The ceiling is fixed in advance rather than being determined by whichever request arrives at HR that afternoon.

Monthly use still needs watching. A cap makes the scheme manageable; it does not prove that every employee using it is financially comfortable. Repeated requests should prompt a private conversation about what is happening, not an assumption that the employee is irresponsible. Sometimes there is a budgeting problem. Sometimes there is a debt problem. Sometimes the pay simply does not stretch far enough.

Brenda, for the 18th, I would take in a proposal to replace the informal scheme rather than defend it as it stands. Your Finance Manager has good reasons to want the current arrangement changed.

Put the proposed rules on one page: the cap, frequency, repayment date, deductions check, request route and who approves. If you do not have a payroll portal, use a standard form and a named approval route. The important thing is that access should not depend on how convincingly someone can explain their hardship in your office.

Then take whatever numbers payroll can give you: requests per month, average amount, total advanced, repeat users, unpaid balances when staff leave and time spent administering it. Ask Finance to help set the overall cash-flow ceiling and agree a review period. Use our experience as a warning about what to monitor, not as proof that your factory will have the same outcome. Reception calls, unplanned absence and supervisors’ time are worth tracking alongside recoveries.

Peter, I think we agree that the informal arrangement needs to end. Where we differ is whether ending advances altogether is the best answer. In our case, closing the window did not end the borrowing or keep the consequences outside the workplace. Written rules and limits turned out to be a better answer than withdrawal.
